title: 90% AI Code Revolution
body:
On July 20, 2023, Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, made a bold prediction in an interview with Bloomberg Technology: "I think we will be there in three to six months, where AI is writing 90% of the code. And then, in 12 months, we may be in a world where AI is writing essentially all of the code."

While such statements often invite skepticism, a recent (29/09/25) blog post by Armin Ronacher, a well-known software developer, suggests this future is not only imminent but, for some, already a reality. This developer, sharing his experience building an infrastructure component, claims to be "probably north of 90% AI-written code."

Ronacher is best known as the creator of widely used and highly influential projects such as the Flask web framework, the Jinja templating engine, and the Werkzeug WSGI utility library. His work has underpinned countless web applications and developer tools, making him a truly accomplished and respected voice in software engineering. When someone of his caliber states, "my current reality is close" to AI writing almost all code, it demands serious attention.

His account is a stark look at the bleeding edge of software engineering, where AI isn't just a helper but a primary code generator. He built a 40,000-line service in Go, including SDKs, YAML, and Pulumi configurations, with AI contributing the vast majority. Yet, he emphasizes a crucial point: "I still treat every line as my responsibility, judged as if I wrote it myself. AI doesn’t change that." This isn't about AI replacing engineers, but rather augmenting them to an unprecedented degree.

A New Workflow: From Rubber Duck to Code Generator

Ronacher's approach to working with AI showcases a profound shift in methodology. He starts with traditional system design and architecture, using AI as "a kind of rubber duck. The back-and-forth helps me see mistakes, even if I don’t need or trust the answers." The real game-changer comes in the code generation phase. He highlights two significant changes in his development stack:

  • Raw SQL: "The fact that I no longer have to write SQL because the AI does it for me is a game changer." He praises its precision, allowing him to bypass ORM limitations and gain clarity in debugging. "It writes solid SQL I could never remember. I just need to review which I can. But to this day I suck at remembering MERGE and WITH when writing it." He also notes, "I also use raw SQL for migrations now."

  • OpenAPI first: "I ended up first generating the OpenAPI specification and then using code generation from there to the interface layer. This approach works better with AI-generated code."

He iterates using multiple AI agents like Claude Code and Codex, each with specific strengths. Claude assists with debugging and tool access ("Claude is indispensable still when debugging and needing a lot of tool access"), while Codex excels at code review ("Codex for code review after PRs. It’s very good at that."). Ronacher describes this synergy: "The working together of the two is where it’s most magical. Claude might find the data, Codex might understand it better."

The Engineer's Evolving Role: Guide, Reviewer, Architect

While AI handles the heavy lifting of code generation, Ronacher stresses that human oversight is more critical than ever. He warns, "I cannot stress enough how bad the code from these agents can be if you’re not careful. While they understand system architecture and how to build something, they can’t keep the whole picture in scope." They might "recreate things that already exist," or "create abstractions that are completely inappropriate for the scale of the problem." The engineer's role transforms into that of a highly skilled guide:

  • Context Provisioner: "You constantly need to learn how to bring the right information to the context." This means "pointing the AI to existing implementations and giving it very specific instructions on how to follow along."

  • Architectural Guardian: Ronacher emphasizes his opinionated approach: "I pay close attention to the fundamentals of system architecture, code layout, and database interaction. I’m incredibly opinionated. As a result, there are certain things I don’t let the AI do." He ensures "there are no weird files that shouldn’t belong there, no duplicate implementations, and no emojis all over the place."

  • Quality Control: "You need to understand your state machines, how the system behaves at any point in time, your database." He cautions, "It is easy to create systems that appear to behave correctly but have unclear runtime behavior when relying on agents." He points out AI's tendency to "love to swallow errors and take away all tracebacks. I’d rather uphold strong invariants and let code crash loudly when they fail, than hide problems. If you don’t fight this, you end up with opaque, unobservable systems."

  • Leveraging AI's Strengths: Despite the pitfalls, the benefits are enormous. Ronacher states, "For me, this has reached the point where I can’t imagine working any other way." He highlights: Rapid Research & Implementation: "Some things that would have taken me a day or two to figure out now take 10 to 15 minutes." This "allows me to directly play with one or two implementations of a problem." Iteration & Refactoring: "I tried three different OpenAPI implementations and approaches in a day." And, "The code looks more organized than it would otherwise have been because the cost of refactoring is quite low." Infrastructure Automation: "Claude got me through AWS and Pulumi. Work I generally dislike became a few days instead of weeks." Adopting New Patterns: "They turned out great at setting up test infrastructure I didn’t know I needed... Claude did it in an hour for all tests."

The Urgent Call to Schools of Computer Science

Armin Ronacher's experience is not an isolated incident; he notes that "some startups are already near 100% AI-generated." He confidently concludes, "Is 90% of code going to be written by AI? I don’t know. What I do know is, that for me, on this project, the answer is already yes. I’m part of that growing subset of developers who are building real systems this way." This reality presents a profound challenge to computer science education.

While many academic institutions are beginning to "think about AI" and introduce "very smart" courses on using tools like ChatGPT to generate pictures or write simple scripts, the industry's vanguard, exemplified by luminaries like Ronacher, is already far beyond this.

The actual demand is not for graduates who can merely use AI as a basic tool, but for those who can work in tandem with agentic AI engineering systems.

As Ronacher states, "none of this removes the need to actually be a good engineer. If you let the AI take over without judgment, you’ll end up with brittle systems and painful surprises."

Our future software engineers need a refined and advanced skillset geared towards this new paradigm:

  1. A strong intuition for LLM behavior: This includes understanding their limitations, peculiarities, and common failure modes. Graduates need to grasp "how LLMs think" to anticipate where they might go wrong and how to course-correct.

  2. Orchestration of AI agents: Moving beyond single-agent interactions, students must learn to manage and coordinate multiple AI tools, each specializing in different tasks (like Claude for debugging and Codex for code review, as Ronacher describes).

  3. Knowledge of various tools for agentic software development: Familiarity with the ecosystem of AI-powered development tools, from code generators and debuggers to testing and infrastructure assistants.

  4. Context Engineering: More encompassing than mere "prompt engineering," this involves skillfully structuring the entire environment—providing relevant existing code, architectural diagrams, specific constraints, and continuous feedback—to guide AI agents effectively towards desired outcomes. This allows AI to be optimally focused on tasks like debugging and code review.

  5. Fundamental knowledge of algorithms, data structures, and software engineering principles: These remain the bedrock upon which effective AI collaboration is built, providing the human engineer with the judgment needed to supervise AI outputs.

The "90% AI-written code" scenario is not a distant prediction; it's here, "just unevenly distributed," and "the number of developers working like this is only going to grow." Educators in computer science have an urgent responsibility to adapt. We must shift our focus from merely introducing AI tools to teaching students how to be the indispensable human partners, architects, and quality guardians in an increasingly AI-driven development landscape. Failing to do so risks producing graduates ill-equipped for the demands of the modern, AI-augmented software industry.
